pharm: Binds growth hormone receptors to stimulate IGF-1 production and direct anabolic, growth-promoting and metabolic effects, including linear bone growth in children.
quick: GH deficiency: non-weight-based start ~0.2 mg/day (0.15-0.3 mg/day) SC, titrate by IGF-1; or weight-based per label
Not relevant (subcutaneous injection); rotate injection sites
Limited data; usually discontinued in pregnancy unless clearly indicated
Limited data; large protein unlikely absorbed orally by infant - use caution
May be used in children with chronic renal insufficiency; monitor
No specific dose; clearance may change in liver disease - titrate by IGF-1
IGF-1, growth velocity, glucose/HbA1c, thyroid function, fundoscopy for intracranial hypertension, scoliosis
summary: Somatropin is recombinant human growth hormone used in children for several causes of growth failure/short stature (GH deficiency, Turner and Noonan syndromes, Prader-Willi syndrome, small-for-gestational-age with no catch-up, idiopathic short stature, chronic renal insufficiency) and in adults for GH deficiency and HIV-associated wasting. It is given by subcutaneous injection with rotating sites and titrated by clinical response and IGF-1. Key safety issues include contraindication in acute critical illness, in severely obese Prader-Willi patients with airway obstruction/sleep apnea, in active malignancy and active proliferative retinopathy, plus monitoring for glucose intolerance, intracranial hypertension, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, scoliosis progression and second neoplasms.
indications: Pediatric growth failure due to inadequate endogenous GH secretion (GH deficiency)
Short stature associated with Turner syndrome or Noonan syndrome
Short stature in children born small for gestational age with no catch-up growth by age 2-4 years
Idiopathic short stature and growth failure in Prader-Willi syndrome and chronic renal insufficiency
Adult growth hormone deficiency and HIV-associated wasting/cachexia (product-dependent)

dosage.d: 0.17 to 0.24 mg/kg/week, divided into equal doses given 6 or 7 days per week
Up to about 0.47 mg/kg/week (Noonan up to ~0.46 mg/kg/week), in divided doses
dosage.n: Higher weekly dosing than classic GH deficiency
Exclude severe obesity, airway obstruction and sleep apnea first (contraindicated)

dosage.d: Non-weight-based: start about 0.2 mg/day (range ~0.15-0.3 mg/day), titrate by IGF-1; or weight-based per product
dosage.n: Use lower starting doses in older or overweight patients; women on oral estrogen may need higher doses

admin: Administer by subcutaneous injection into the back of the upper arm, abdomen, buttock, or thigh, rotating sites regularly to avoid lipoatrophy
Reconstitute/prepare per the specific product instructions; do not shake vigorously
Refrigerate as directed and check the product for clarity before injection
Titrate dose to clinical response, growth velocity (children) and serum IGF-1, avoiding levels above the age/sex-specific normal range
Use the lowest effective dose, especially when initiating adult therapy
moa: Somatropin binds dimeric growth hormone receptors on target cell membranes, triggering intracellular signal transduction and transcription of GH-dependent proteins including IGF-1, IGF binding protein-3 and the acid-labile subunit. It has direct tissue and metabolic effects and indirect effects mediated by IGF-1: stimulation of chondrocyte differentiation and proliferation (linear bone growth in children with open epiphyses), increased protein synthesis and lean body mass, lipolysis, and increased hepatic glucose output with reduced insulin sensitivity.

absolute: Acute critical illness after open-heart or abdominal surgery, multiple accidental trauma, or acute respiratory failure (increased mortality)
Severely obese Prader-Willi syndrome patients or those with upper airway obstruction, sleep apnea, or severe respiratory impairment (risk of sudden death)
Active proliferative or severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Known hypersensitivity to somatropin or excipients
relative: History of childhood cancer (risk of second neoplasm)
monitor: Funduscopy for intracranial hypertension; hip/knee complaints and scoliosis in children

preg: There are limited data on somatropin use in pregnancy; endogenous growth hormone is normally replaced by placental variant during gestation. Treatment is generally discontinued during pregnancy unless clearly required. Discuss continuation with an endocrinologist.
lact: There is little information on somatropin in breast milk; as a large protein it is unlikely to be absorbed intact by a nursing infant, but use caution and weigh the mother's clinical need.
renal: Somatropin is indicated in children with growth failure due to chronic renal insufficiency (up to the time of renal transplantation); monitor renal osteodystrophy and growth. No standard adult dose reduction is specified, but titrate by IGF-1.
hepatic: No specific dosing recommendation is given for hepatic impairment; growth hormone clearance can be altered in liver disease, so titrate cautiously to IGF-1 and clinical response.

major: Glucocorticoids/corticosteroids (inhibit the growth-promoting effect; somatropin may unmask central adrenal insufficiency requiring steroid dose adjustment)
moderate: Insulin and oral antidiabetic agents (may need dose increases due to reduced insulin sensitivity)
Oral estrogens in women (may require higher somatropin doses)
CYP450-metabolized drugs such as some sex steroids, corticosteroids, anticonvulsants and ciclosporin (clearance can change as somatropin can increase CYP3A4 activity)
minor: Thyroid hormone (somatropin may unmask central hypothyroidism, altering levothyroxine needs)
interactions.diagnostics: Increases serum IGF-1; can raise glucose/HbA1c and lower free thyroxine by increasing T4-to-T3 conversion.

serious: Glucose intolerance / new or worsened diabetes mellitus
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis and progression of scoliosis (children)
Increased mortality in acute critical illness
Second neoplasms in childhood cancer survivors
rare: Sudden death in at-risk Prader-Willi patients
emergency: Severe intracranial hypertension with visual loss

monitoring: Serum IGF-1 (keep within age/sex normal range) and growth velocity
Funduscopy at initiation and if symptoms; monitor for limp/hip-knee pain and scoliosis in children
counsel: Give the injection under the skin and rotate sites (tummy, thigh, upper arm, buttock) to protect the skin
Tell the doctor about persistent headaches, changes in vision, or nausea/vomiting (could signal raised pressure in the head)
Report any new limp or hip/knee pain in a child, or worsening curve of the back
Watch for increased thirst, urination, or tiredness that may suggest high blood sugar
Store the medicine in the fridge as instructed and never use it if it looks cloudy or discolored
pk: IGF-1 rises within hours; clinical growth response over weeks to months
Subcutaneous peak serum concentration at approximately 3-4 hours
Subcutaneous apparent half-life about 2-3 hours (longer than IV due to slow absorption)
Once-daily/6-7-days-weekly dosing sustains the biological effect via IGF-1
Refrigerate at 2-8 C; protect from light and do not freeze - follow product-specific in-use stability
pearls: Titrate to IGF-1 within the age/sex normal range and to growth velocity, not to a fixed level
Contraindicated in acute critical illness - pharmacologic doses increased mortality in ICU patients
Screen Prader-Willi patients for obesity, airway obstruction and sleep apnea before starting (sudden death reported)
Can reduce insulin sensitivity and unmask central hypothyroidism or adrenal insufficiency - monitor glucose, thyroid and cortisol
Watch children for slipped capital femoral epiphysis, scoliosis progression and pseudotumor cerebri
missed: If a dose is missed, give it as soon as remembered the same day; if it is not remembered until the next day, skip the missed dose and resume the usual schedule. Do not give a double dose.
overdose: Acute overdose could initially cause hypoglycemia followed by hyperglycemia. Long-term excess produces signs of acromegaly/gigantism and growth-hormone excess (fluid retention, organomegaly). Management is supportive with blood-glucose monitoring and correction; review and reduce dosing.
